title-group.article-title: Evaluating drug interaction potential from cytokine release syndrome using a physiologically based pharmacokinetic model: A case study of teclistamab

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) was associated with teclistamab treatment in the phase I/II MajesTEC‐1 study. Cytokines, especially interleukin (IL)‐6, are known suppressors of cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes' activity. A physiologically based pharmacokinetic model evaluated the impact of IL‐6 serum levels on exposure of substrates of various CYP enzymes (1A2, 2C9, 2C19, 3A4, 3A5). Two IL‐6 kinetics profiles were assessed, the mean IL‐6 profile with a maximum concentration (C max) of IL‐6 (21 pg/mL) and the IL‐6 profile of the patient presenting the highest IL‐6 C max (288 pg/mL) among patients receiving the recommended phase II dose of teclistamab in MajesTEC‐1. For the mean IL‐6 kinetics profile, teclistamab was predicted to result in a limited change in exposure of CYP substrates (area under the curve [AUC] mean ratio 0.87–1.20). For the maximum IL‐6 kinetics profile, the impact on omeprazole, simvastatin, midazolam, and cyclosporine exposure was weak to moderate (mean AUC ratios 1.90–2.23), and minimal for caffeine and s‐warfarin (mean AUC ratios 0.82–1.25). Maximum change in exposure for these substrates occurred 3–4 days after step‐up dosing in cycle 1. These results suggest that after cycle 1, drug interaction from IL‐6 effect has no meaningful impact on CYP activities, with minimal or moderate impact on CYP substrates. The highest risk of drug interaction is expected to occur during step‐up dosing up to 7 days after the first treatment dose (1.5 mg/kg subcutaneously) and during and after CRS.

p.bold: WHAT IS THE CURRENT KNOWLEDGE ON THE TOPIC?

boxed-text.p:
CRS, which may modulate the activity of CYP450 enzymes, is associated with the BCMA×CD3 bispecific antibody, teclistamab.
WHAT QUESTION DID THIS STUDY ADDRESS?

What is the impact of IL‐6 serum levels resulting from CRS associated with teclistamab on exposure of co‐administered CYP450 substrates? What is the impact on CRS management medications?
WHAT DOES THIS STUDY ADD TO OUR KNOWLEDGE?

PBPK modeling can be used to evaluate the effects of IL‐6 on CYP450 activities. After teclistamab administration, a drug interaction from indirect IL‐6 changes, secondary to CRS, can affect CYP450 activities but had no meaningful clinical significance, with minimal or moderate impact on CYP450 substrates under these conditions.
HOW MIGHT THIS CHANGE DRUG DISCOVERY, DEVELOPMENT, AND/OR THERAPEUTICS?

This study demonstrates the viability of a PBPK model evaluating the impact of IL‐6 levels after teclistamab administration on exposure of different CYP450 substrates. This modeling approach together with the profile of CRS formed the basis of recommendations in the product label for monitoring up to 7 days after the first treatment dose or during a CRS event in patients receiving concomitant medications.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Immunologically active proteins including interferons (IFNs), interleukins (ILs), and other cytokines are produced in response to infection or inflammation, and their systemic levels are elevated in chronic and acute inflammatory conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA) or cytokine release syndrome (CRS). 1 , 2 Cytokines have been shown to alter the activity of cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes by affecting their stability or transcription factor activity for CYP enzyme expression, including PXR and CAR. 3 , 4 Because monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), growth factors, cytokine modulators, and other therapeutic proteins (TPs) are not directly metabolized by CYP enzymes, they are generally perceived to have little to no involvement in metabolism‐based drug interactions; consequently, TP‐drug interactions (TP‐DI) are often considered to be clinically insignificant. However, the effects on CYP enzyme activities resulting from the systemic cytokine changes driven by TPs can impact exposure of comedication metabolized by CYP enzymes. 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8

Among cytokines released during CRS and other inflammatory states, IL‐6 is the best known potent suppressor of CYP enzyme activity. 2 , 9 For example, in vitro studies have demonstrated that IL‐6 incubated at physiological concentrations led to decreased expression or activity of CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP3A4, and CYP3A5 in human hepatocytes. 3 , 10 Importantly, this change in CYP activity has been confirmed clinically in patients with RA, who present IL‐6 systemic concentrations ~50 pg/mL, and with higher exposure in CYP substrates compared with healthy patients. 11 , 12 Administration of TPs that are cytokine modulators, such as the anti‐IL‐6 receptor mAb tocilizumab or the anti‐IL‐6 mAbs sirukumab and siltuximab, leads to restoration of CYP enzyme activity in patients with RA, despite an observed elevation in systemic IL‐6 levels. 8 , 13 , 14

CRS commonly occurs following administration of immunotherapies. Teclistamab is the first approved B‐cell maturation antigen (BCMA) × CD3 bispecific antibody with flexible, weight‐based dosing for the treatment of triple‐class exposed (TCE) relapsed/refractory (RR) multiple myeloma (MM). 15 , 16 It redirects CD3+ T cells to mediate T‐cell activation and subsequent lysis of BCMA‐expressing MM cells. 17 , 18 The accelerated approval of teclistamab was based on the pivotal portion of the phase I/II MajesTEC‐1 trial (NCT03145181/NCT04557098), which assessed the efficacy and safety of teclistamab at the recommended phase II dose (RP2D; once weekly 1.5 mg/kg subcutaneous) in patients with TCE RRMM. 19 To minimize the risk of CRS, teclistamab is administered using two step‐up doses (0.06 and 0.3 mg/kg) prior to the first treatment dose (1.5 mg/kg). Of the 165 patients who received the RP2D across the dose escalation and expansion portions of MajesTEC‐1, 119 patients (72.1%) experienced CRS, all but 1 of which were grade 1/2. 19 Because CRS was sometimes associated with an increase in systemic IL‐6, a risk assessment of potential DI on CYP enzymes following teclistamab treatment was explored.

In 2023, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued a guidance for sponsors to determine the need for drug–drug interaction (DDI) studies for TPs by providing a systematic, risk‐based approach, including recommendations for DDI assessment tools such as physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling. 20 PBPK models are based on the physicochemical and kinetic properties of a compound and the physiology of a population. This modeling framework can be used to simulate drug exposure, mechanistically quantify pharmacokinetics, explore DDIs, and inform dosing strategies. 21 , 22 PBPK modeling has been previously applied to CYP‐mediated TP‐DI or disease‐DI 8 ; for instance, the impact of changes in systemic levels of IL‐6 on exposure of CYP substrates has been effectively predicted using PBPK modeling in patients with RA 11 , 12 or other inflammatory diseases, 23 COVID‐19 patients presenting with cytokine storm, 24 and patients treated with cytokine modulators. 13 , 25 , 26 , 27 , 28

Here, we report an analysis to evaluate the impact of IL‐6 serum levels observed after teclistamab administration in MajesTEC‐1 on the predicted exposure of concomitant CYP substrates caffeine (CYP1A2), s‐warfarin (CYP2C9), omeprazole (CYP2C19), midazolam (CYP3A4), cyclosporine (CYP3A5), and simvastatin (CYP3A4) using a PBPK modeling approach. Additionally, the time to reach the maximum change in CYP activity due to IL‐6 and the return to 80% of the baseline enzymatic activity was evaluated, with the start of step‐up dosing in cycle 1 as reference; 80% of the baseline enzymatic activity was considered as a reasonable cutoff at which DDI liability would be low. This work was performed to provide additional information on the potential for teclistamab to cause DDI with CYP substrates, including a quantitative assessment of the effects of teclistamab‐induced CRS on CYP enzyme activities. This work provided guidance on the timing of the highest DDI potential.

sec.title: Clinical study design
sec.p: The full study design of the MajesTEC‐1 trial has been reported previously. 18 , 19 MajesTEC‐1 enrolled adult patients who had RRMM per International Myeloma Working Group criteria 29 , 30 with disease progression at screening after triple‐class exposure to an immunomodulatory drug, a proteasome inhibitor, and an anti‐CD38 mAb. Previous treatment with a BCMA‐targeted therapy was not allowed. The current analysis is based on data from patients who received the RP2D (approved dose) in the MajesTEC‐1 trial (data cutoff: March 16, 2022).

In this study, subjects received two step‐up doses (0.06 and 0.3 mg/kg) prior to the first treatment dose (1.5 mg/kg) of teclistamab. Each dose triggered a slight elevation of systemic IL‐6 concentrations (2‐ to 4‐fold of the baseline, based on the mean IL‐6 profile). Cycle 1, corresponding to the first treatment dose, started 168 h after the first step‐up dose, and the peak of IL‐6 concentrations in cycle 1 was observed 48 h after the start of cycle 1 (i.e., 216 h after the first step‐up dose). When a patient experienced CRS, administration of the anti‐IL‐6 receptor mAb, tocilizumab, was permitted to inhibit the IL‐6 signaling pathway and promote an anti‐inflammatory effect.

The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and the Good Clinical Practice guidelines of the International Council for Harmonization. The study protocol, amendments, and relevant documents were approved by the local independent ethics committee or institutional review board at each study site. All the patients provided written informed consent.

sec.title: Software
sec.p: The modeling and simulations were performed using SimCYP version 21 (SimCYP Ltd, a Certara company, Sheffield, UK). The IL‐6 model was reconstructed based on literature, 13 , 14 and the caffeine, S‐warfarin, omeprazole, midazolam, simvastatin and cyclosporin compound files from SimCYP v21 were used. These compounds are considered sensitive probes for their corresponding CYP enzymes, per FDA guidance. 31 The percentage of involvement of the major CYP‐mediated pathway in the metabolism of these substrates was verified by SimCYP 32 : caffeine, CYP1A2; S‐warfarin, CYP2C9; omeprazole, CYP2C19; simvastatin, CYP3A4; cyclosporine and midazolam, CYP3A4 and CYP3A5.

sec.title: IL‐6 PBPK model and simulation design
sec.p: A PBPK model of IL‐6 was developed based on preexisting models available in the literature. 10 , 11 , 13 As IL‐6 is an endogenous protein, the appearance of IL‐6 in the body was modeled via IV infusion. The IL‐6 amount produced varies across individual patients, and the dosing regimen must therefore be adjusted to recover the observed IL‐6 kinetics data for each clinical study. Distribution was modeled by a minimal PBPK model, and the elimination was non‐mechanistically modeled. Interaction parameters of IL‐6 toward CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP3A4 and CYP3A5 were derived from a previously published in vitro study. 10 A suppression effect was modeled for all studied CYP enzymes, except for CYP1A2 for which an induction effect is modeled based on clinical data. 13 The input parameters used in the model are described in Table 1. 10 , 11 , 13 Although observed IL‐6 concentrations were measured in serum, plasma IL‐6 concentrations were simulated. Since serum and plasma have similar volume, simulating plasma concentrations instead of serum has a negligible impact on the predictions.

sec.p:
The IL‐6 PBPK model was then used to evaluate the impact of IL‐6 plasma levels on the exposure of different CYP substrates. The interaction was modeled by incorporating a modulation effect on the level of CYP proteins in the liver, assuming that the IL‐6 concentration would affect the rate of enzyme synthesis in the liver. 11 , 12 Because IL‐6 was administered via IV infusion, its enzymatic modulation potency consequently affected only the enzymatic activity in the liver; distribution of IL‐6 from systemic circulation to the gut is not captured by the software. To account for the effect on gut enzymatic activity, the following steps, also described in the literature, 11 were applied to calculate the impact of IL‐6 on CYP substrate exposure:
In Run 1, simulations of IL‐6 + probe substrate were performed until steady‐state or baseline level of enzyme activity was reached, and the maximum impact on the enzymatic activity in the liver was noted. ○
In the population section, abundance of the corresponding enzyme in the intestine and colon was reduced by the percentage of remaining activity observed in the liver (Table S1).
Run 2 was performed by repeating Run 1 with the adjusted population. The overall impact of IL‐6 on the exposure of the probe was calculated from the ratio of mean maximum concentration (C max) or area under the curve (AUC) from time zero to infinity (AUCinf) from the inhibition arm of Run 2 over the control arm of Run 1. Because omeprazole presents mechanism‐based inhibition (MBI) toward CYP2C19, simulations with MBI turned off were first used to assess the impact of IL‐6 concentrations only toward CYP2C19 activity for transient peak IL‐6 concentrations. ○
For Run 2, MBI of CYP2C19 was turned on again, with changes in CYP2C19 abundance due to IL‐6 applied to the intestine and colon, as described above.

This stepwise approach has been previously applied in similar PBPK modeling evaluations of TP‐DI for patients with RA exposed to cytokine modulators. The IL‐6 PBPK model was calibrated and validated using the assumption that serum IL‐6 concentrations were representative of hepatic IL‐6 concentrations, and therefore were driving the interaction on CYP substrates. Simulations reported here were performed in a population of healthy volunteers. 11 , 12 The coefficient of variation (CV) for liver CYP3A4 abundance was modified from 41% to 33%, 33 and the CV for liver CYP2C9 for extensive metabolizers was changed from 64% to 18% based on published data. 34 , 35 , 36

sec.title: Model verification
sec.p: Model performance was verified by comparing the predicted kinetics of IL‐6 alone (transient peak or at steady‐state concentrations of 50 pg/mL) with the observed data (Figure S1). The IL‐6 dosing regimen was adjusted in the trial design component of the PBPK modeling framework to recover the observed IL‐6 kinetic profile, further described in Supplemental Methods. The performance of the IL‐6 model to predict CYP‐mediated TP‐DI was evaluated in previous studies. 13 , 14 Patients with RA who had systemic IL‐6 levels of 50 pg/mL received a single dose of caffeine, omeprazole, s‐warfarin, midazolam, 37 or simvastatin, 14 with or without the anti‐IL‐6 receptor mAb tocilizumab or the anti‐IL‐6 mAb sirukumab (Table S2 and Figure S2). Exposure of the probe in the presence of IL‐6 was compared with that in the presence of tocilizumab or sirukumab. Observed clinical data available in RA patients correspond to the condition IL‐6 CYP inactivation on, mimicking the IL‐6 effect at 50 pg/mL; in the presence of tocilizumab or sirukumab, data correspond to the condition IL‐6 CYP inactivation off, mimicking the IL‐6 effect at 0 pg/mL.

sec.title: Prospective simulations
sec.p: Prospective simulations were performed using observed IL‐6 data from patients in MajesTEC‐1 who had an IL‐6 C max occurring before tocilizumab administration, or who did not receive any tocilizumab in cycle 1 of teclistamab treatment. A maximum of 112 of the 119 patients who experienced CRS are included in the analysis, because not all patients were sampled at all time points. The impact of IL‐6 concentrations on the aforementioned CYP substrates (i.e., caffeine, s‐warfarin, omeprazole, midazolam, and simvastatin) was evaluated, with administration of the CYP substrate as single dose when peak change in enzymatic activity was reached. Cyclosporine, a CYP3A4 and CYP3A5 substrate and a drug that patients with RRMM may receive, was also included in the analysis.

Simulations were performed using two IL‐6 kinetics profiles: Scenario 1 was the mean IL‐6 concentration per time event up to cycle 1 day 15, where mean C max = 21 pg/mL, and scenario 2 was the highest individual observed concentration of IL‐6 (288 pg/mL) among all patients occurring during cycle 1, before any administration of tocilizumab following the teclistamab RP2D in MajesTEC‐1, representing the worst‐case scenario for DI liability.

Ten trials of 75 subjects (aged 20–50 years, 50% female) were simulated for both scenarios. The IL‐6 dosing regimen was adjusted to recover the observed IL‐6 kinetics profile for the two scenarios (Table S3). Substrate exposure (C max and AUCinf) ratios were computed for each simulated trial, corresponding to the ratio of CYP substrate C max or AUC in the presence (inhibition arm of Run 2) over the absence (control arm of Run 1) of IL‐6. The mean exposure ratios from the 10 trials were reported for scenarios 1 and 2.

In addition to assessing the impact of IL‐6 levels on the exposure of different CYP substrates, the time to reach the maximum change in CYP activity as a result of IL‐6 and the return to 80% of the baseline enzymatic activity was evaluated, with the start of cycle 1 as reference; 80% of the baseline enzymatic activity was considered as a reasonable cutoff at which the impact on exposures would be considered low.

sec.title: Model performance evaluation
sec.p:
Simulation performance was evaluated by applying the Guest et al. 38 success prediction criteria, enabling tighter boundaries for AUC and C max ratios close to 1. The limits of success coalesce when the observed ratio (R obs) is 1 and eventually approach the traditional twofold limits as the ratio becomes larger: upper limit=Robs×limit
lower limit=Robslimit
limit=δ+xRobs−1Robs

In this analysis, R obs represents AUC+inhibitor/AUCcontrol, x represents the fold difference (set to 2), and δ accounts for variability in the observed data, where the more stringent criterion (δ = 1) is applied.

sec.title: Model verification
sec.p: The transient peak and steady‐state concentrations of IL‐6 were well captured by the model (Figures S3 and S4). The observed C max and AUCinf ratios for the different substrates were well predicted by the model, with a trend of a slight overprediction for the AUC ratio (a maximum of 16% for s‐warfarin). The C max ratio for simvastatin was slightly underpredicted. However, the predicted C max and AUC ratio met the predefined success criteria, giving confidence in the current IL‐6 model to prospectively predict the impact of cytokine exposure on the studied CYP substrates metabolized by these CYPs (Table S4).

sec.title: Simulation of IL‐6 kinetics from MajesTEC‐1
sec.p: The simulated and observed IL‐6 systemic concentration profiles from patients enrolled in MajesTEC‐1 until cycle 1 day 15 with the aforementioned criteria are shown in Figure 1. Baseline IL‐6 was captured by the model, in addition to the multiple peaks of IL‐6, including after the two step‐up doses. The observed data (mean IL‐6 kinetic profile and IL‐6 kinetic profile of the patient with the highest C max) were well captured. The IL‐6 kinetics profile of the patient with the highest C max (scenario 2) was not captured by the predicted variability of the IL‐6 kinetics profile when the mean IL‐6 kinetics profile was simulated (scenario 1). This result justifies a separate simulation for scenario 2, with an adapted dosing regimen to recover the observed kinetics profile.

sec.title: Predictions with IL‐6 as a perpetrator of CYP substrates
sec.p: Using the PBPK model, the mean IL‐6 kinetics profile (scenario 1, mean C max = 21 pg/mL) following teclistamab administered at the RP2D was predicted to result in a limited change in exposure of caffeine, s‐warfarin, omeprazole, midazolam, cyclosporine, and simvastatin substrates (mean AUC ratio = 0.87–1.20) (Table 2). When the IL‐6 kinetics profile with the highest C max (scenario 2, IL‐6 C max = 288 pg/mL) was considered, the impact on the exposure was predicted to be moderate for omeprazole and simvastatin (mean AUC ratio = 2.23 and 2.09, respectively), and weak for midazolam and cyclosporine (mean AUC ratio = 1.90), and the impact on the exposure of caffeine and s‐warfarin substrates was predicted to be minimal (mean AUC ratio = 0.82 and 1.25, respectively).

sec.p: For the mean IL‐6 profile, the lowest minimum level of CYP activity was for omeprazole (CYP2C19) at 87%, and the highest maximum was for caffeine (CYP1A2) at 118%. This maximum difference was observed at 65–82 h (3 days) after the start of cycle 1 (Table 3 and Figure 2). For the profile with the highest IL‐6 C max, the lowest minimum level of CYP activity was for omeprazole (CYP2C19) at 56%, and the highest maximum was for caffeine (CYP1A2) at 128%. This maximum difference was observed at 75 h (3 days) to 105 h (4 days) after the start of cycle 1. For the profile with the highest IL‐6 C max, a return to 80% of the baseline enzymatic activity was observed 7–8 days after the start of cycle 1 (full treatment dose, 1.5 mg/kg teclistamab). When simvastatin and omeprazole, both presenting a moderate inhibition at peak of IL‐6, were administered at the corresponding enzymatic activity of 80% of baseline, the predicted AUC mean ratios for simvastatin and omeprazole were equal to 1.45 and 1.47, respectively, which corresponds to a weak interaction.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: CRS is a common adverse event observed following the administration of many T‐cell immunotherapies, resulting in elevated levels of inflammatory cytokines such as IL‐6, a known suppressor of CYP enzymes. 1 , 2 , 9 PBPK modeling has previously been applied to CYP‐mediated TP‐DI evaluation (e.g., for direct IL‐6 modulators) successfully predicting observed changes in the exposure of CYP substrates in the context of changes in systemic levels of IL‐6. 11 , 12 , 13 , 23 , 24 , 25 Here, we used a PBPK modeling approach to explore the potential impact of multiple transient peaks of IL‐6 on CYP activity due to CRS following treatment with teclistamab. As verification, our model accurately captured the increase in IL‐6 levels (transient peak, steady‐state concentration at 50 pg/mL) observed in other clinical studies reported in the literature 13 , 14 , 25 , 28 and predicted the modulator effect of steady‐state IL‐6 levels on specific CYP substrates. 13 , 14

Because no observed DI data between CYP substrates and transient peaks of IL‐6 were identified in the literature, verification of the model performance to predict a DI liability was performed at steady‐state concentration of IL‐6 rather than in the presence of a transient peak. In addition, change in exposure of CYP substrates where CYP3A4, CYP3A5, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, and CYP1A2 pathways are mainly involved were included in this evaluation, because of the availability of corresponding clinical DDI data in the literature. 13 , 14 Although changes in other CYP activities have been studied in vitro, no corresponding clinical data are available to verify the inhibitor potency of IL‐6 toward these CYP pathways. An exception is CYP2D6, which was not included in the analysis, but whose substrate has shown no change in exposure in patients with RA based on AUC. 11 Combined, the robustness of the model and resultant predictions give confidence in the application of the model to assess the impact of transient peaks of IL‐6 as a perpetrator of CYP450 substrates, providing validity to these results.

In this analysis, the PBPK modeling and simulation results suggest that the DI effects of IL‐6 on CYP activities following the administration of a TP that mediates a cytokine storm have no meaningful clinical significance, with minimal or moderate impact on CYP substrates up to 7 days after the first treatment dose of 1.5 mg/kg teclistamab in cycle 1 or during a CRS event. The mean IL‐6 kinetics profile was predicted to result in a limited change in exposure of substrates, and the highest predicted mean AUC ratio was 1.20 for omeprazole and simvastatin. When the profile of the patient with the highest C max (288 pg/mL) was considered, with peak IL‐6 ~ 10‐fold higher than the observed mean IL‐6 profile, the impact was weak to moderate on the exposure of omeprazole, midazolam, simvastatin, and cyclosporine (1.90 ≤ mean AUC ratio ≤ 2.23) and minimal for caffeine and s‐warfarin (mean AUC ratio = 0.82 and 1.25, respectively). For both scenarios, the maximum change in exposure for the studied substrates occurred 3–4 days after the start of cycle 1 (i.e., first full treatment dose), and a return to 80% of the baseline enzymatic activity took approximately 7 days after the start of cycle 1 for the patient with the highest IL‐6 C max, associated with a weak interaction.

In a similar study following blinatumomab treatment where a single peak of IL‐6 concentrations (~1600 pg/mL) was observed, PBPK model predictions demonstrated a maximum interaction of 1.9, corresponding to the observed AUC ratio of simvastatin. 28 In contrast, our model predicted a 2.09 AUC ratio for simvastatin, with 5.6‐fold lower peak IL‐6 concentrations of 288 pg/mL. A potential explanation may be differences in the IL‐6 kinetics profiles following blinatumomab versus teclistamab administration. The time to reach peak IL‐6 after subcutaneous teclistamab was 48 h, while the peak was achieved only 6 h after continuous intravenous infusion of blinatumomab. 28 Consequently, we simulated a longer time of infusion to recover IL‐6 levels after teclistamab dosing, resulting in an increased duration of CYP substrate inactivation and increased time to restore CYP baseline activity. Further, our analysis was designed to not only capture the highest peak of IL‐6 observed in cycle 1 but also the initial baseline levels of IL‐6 in patients, as well as the slight increase of IL‐6 because of the two step‐up doses. Therefore, the approach presented here accounts for accumulation over the time of inactivation, which may explain the increased extent of the interaction. In addition, model prediction with the mean IL‐6 profile led to minimal changes in CYP‐mediated clearance (AUC ratio < 1.25), consistent with the observation that impacts on CYP substrate exposure because of IL‐6 are generally less than twofold, rarely leading to significant drug interactions. 5 Recently, an analogous PBPK modeling approach was used to assess the DDI potential with CYP substrates owing to transient increase in IL‐6 levels after mosunetuzumab 26 and glofitamab 27 administration. Comparable to the teclistamab work reported here, both models predicted the DDI liability for similar CYP substrates (3A4 only for mosunetuzumab and 1A2, 2C9, and 3A5 for glofitamab), considering the mean (or median) and the 95th percentile (or the highest) of IL‐6 kinetics profile observed after mosunetuzumab and glofitamab administration. In these analyses, in the worst case, increase in CYP substrates was also ≤2‐fold. To assess the duration of enzyme suppression, DDI simulations at different points in time were reported for mosunetuzumab, with the same pattern as our predicted DDI liability when enzymatic activity was back to 80% of the baseline. Some differences between these modeling works may rely on the different IL‐6 kinetics plasma profile observed after mosunetuzumab, glofitamab, and teclistamab administration. Multiple increases of IL‐6 plasma concentrations by ~4‐ to 10‐fold compared with mean baseline were observed during the first cycle of treatment with mosunetuzumab and by ~10‐fold in the step‐up dosing regimen for glofitamab, corresponding to a slightly different IL‐6 kinetic plasma profile than the one observed after teclistamab administration. After teclistamab administration, less frequent and less intense IL‐6 elevations were observed, with two slight increases by 2‐ to 4‐fold after the respective step‐up doses, followed by a more pronounced 10‐fold increase after the first treatment dose (based on the mean profile).

The key aspects of the modeling and simulation work presented here are the predictions of the DDI liability on CYP1A2, 2C9, 3A4, 3A5, and 2C19 substrates at the minimum enzymatic activity level and at 80% of the baseline activity (with the associated time to return to 80% of the baseline activity) considering the mean and the highest IL‐6 kinetics plasma profile observed after the two step‐up doses and the first treatment dose of teclistamab. The outcomes of this work were shared with the FDA in 2022 upon their request for additional information about DDI potential with CYP substrates after teclistamab administration, including a quantitative assessment of the effects of teclistamab‐induced CRS on CYP enzyme activities. 39 In the NDA review of antibodies for which similar PBPK evaluation was performed (blinatumomab in 2014, mosunetuzumab and glofitamab in 2023), it is stated that “the PBPK model prediction cannot adequately address drug interaction potential of blinatumomab, as an exposure‐response relationship between IL‐6 plasma levels and change in CYP activities in humans has not been established” 40 and that “PBPK analyses are considered inadequate to evaluate drug interaction potential of mosunetuzumab and duration of its effect on CYP3A substrates because exposure‐response relationships between cytokines and CYP3A activity in human have not been established.” 41 For glofitamab, a similar conclusion on the PBPK modeling work as for mosunetuzumab was drawn; however, recommendation on the monitoring period for drug interaction liability was performed based on “reviewer's evaluation of the available clinical data in the literature, understanding of postulated mechanism of IL‐6 mediated CYP suppression and estimated time of CYP recovery”. 42 For teclistamab, the NDA review in 2022 (1 year before mosunetuzumab and glofitamab NDA review) concluded that “the available cytokine data, the profile of CRS and the predictions from the Applicant's PBPK model all suggest the highest risk of DDI is expected to occur early during treatment with teclistamab (up to approximately 1 week after the first treatment dose) and during and after CRS.” Limitations of the PBPK modeling exercise were also reported, such as the evaluation of only IL‐6 effects on CYP activity and lack of sensitivity analysis on interaction parameters. The acceptance of the PBPK modeling and simulation to address potential DDI liability on CYP substrates after antibody administration might be case‐specific, depending on the duration and the magnitude of interleukin increase. In the case of teclistamab, a single high peak of IL‐6 in a limited timeframe in the context of CRS after teclistamab administration, in combination with the predictions of the magnitude of the DDI when CYP activity is at 80% of the baseline activity, and the predictions of the time frame of the suppression, may have contributed to the conclusion regarding the time period for the highest risk of DDI.

Teclistamab can not only cause an increase in IL‐6 but also increases the levels of IL‐2 receptors and IL‐10. 15 Our analysis focused on the impact of IL‐6 on CYP activity and does not take the additional cytokines into account, like recently published PBPK modeling studies. 24 , 28 IL‐2, but not IL‐10, has demonstrated CYP suppression in vitro, albeit to a lesser extent than IL‐6. 3 , 28 , 43 No information is available for IL‐2 receptors. While there has been a clear link established both in vitro and clinically between changes in IL‐6 and CYP modulation, a direct effect of other cytokines such as IL‐2 and IL‐10 on CYP enzymes remains to be conclusively confirmed clinically. 5 , 44 , 45 Nevertheless, based on limited data, it can be concluded that synergistic effects of IL‐6 with other cytokines would likely lead to a similar effect on CYP activities as IL‐6 alone. 5

High interpatient variability was observed in the IL‐6 kinetics profile, with a 10‐fold difference between the mean C max and the highest C max, inherent to the variability in the rate and extent of IL‐6 produced during the cytokine storm after teclistamab administration, which could not be captured by the model. To compensate for this limitation, typical and worst‐case scenarios of IL‐6 kinetics were evaluated separately, corresponding to the typical and maximum DDI liability that can be expected, respectively, based on these selected patients.

In conclusion, PBPK modeling and simulation results suggest that the effect of IL‐6 increases induced by teclistamab on CYP activities has no meaningful clinical significance, with minimal or moderate impact on CYP substrates. Results suggest that the highest risk of altering CYP enzymes through a cytokine storm is from the initiation of teclistamab step‐up dose 1 up to 7 days after the first treatment dose or during a CRS event.
